Koh-Lanta — Survival, Progression and Victory Analysis

1. History and Scope

Koh-Lanta has aired since 2001. In 2026, TF1 presents the show’s 33rd season, titled Les Reliques du Destin. The analysis, however, covers 17 selected seasons and 340 contestants. All-Star editions and hybrid formats were excluded because returning contestants’ experience, reputation and pre-existing relationships make observations less comparable. Some seasons structured from the outset around age or gender were also excluded to avoid confusing the individual effect of these variables with the effect of production-imposed tribe composition. Finally, seasons were not retained when exits, returns to the game or elimination mechanisms could not be reconstructed reliably enough.

2. Research Question

To what extent are age, gender and physical profile associated with a contestant’s journey in Koh-Lanta, from the earliest eliminations through the final stages and victory?

This study aims to identify trends and statistical associations, not to establish with certainty the causes of eliminations or victories. Few observed differences reach the conventional threshold of statistical significance. The analysis includes 340 contestants, but only 17 seasons serve as the contextual units being compared, which limits the strength and generalizability of the conclusions.

This caution is even more important for the final stages—orienteering, the pole challenge and the final jury—because they involve only a small subset of contestants. The corresponding estimates can therefore change substantially based on only a few individual journeys. When a p-value is greater than 0.05, the observed difference is not statistically established and should be interpreted as an exploratory trend rather than a confirmed result.

All results presented below should therefore be read with caution, especially those concerning the final phase and those associated with a p-value above 0.05. They are useful for generating hypotheses, but they do not demonstrate causal relationships or establish general rules about Koh-Lanta.

3. Selected Variables

Age

Age may influence recovery, endurance, resistance to deprivation and injury risk. Younger contestants may have physical advantages, but also less social or strategic experience. Older contestants may be more exposed to fatigue while benefiting from greater emotional stability and a better understanding of relationships. The initial intuition was therefore that the effect of age might vary across the different phases of the show.

Gender

Gender may be associated with performance in certain challenges, but also with how physical usefulness, one’s role within the tribe or strategic threat are perceived. Some challenges favor strength or speed, while others depend more on balance, precision, endurance or concentration. The initial hypothesis was not that one gender would always have an advantage, but that differences could change across phases.

Physical Profile

Physical profile was selected because bodily abilities play an important role in Koh-Lanta. An athletic contestant may be useful to the tribe and better protected during the earliest eliminations. After the merge—the point when the tribes come together and the competition becomes primarily individual—the same contestant may instead be viewed as a threat. The initial hypothesis was therefore that a physical profile could provide an early advantage, then lose importance or become a strategic liability later.

The physical variable is more difficult to measure than age or gender. An initial automation attempt used occupations, biographies and available references to sporting activity, but the results did not always match observable reality. The classification was therefore performed manually, contestant by contestant, based on sporting background, occupation, apparent build, muscularity and biographical information. This human-in-the-loop approach corrected errors from a purely automated classification, but the variable remains less standardized and partly subjective. Results involving this variable should therefore be interpreted with additional caution.

4. Understanding Exit Types

Tribal Council

Tribal Council is the main elimination mechanism. Contestants vote to decide which player must leave the game. Exits linked to paired fates are included in this category when a vote against one member also causes the partner’s elimination.

Injury / Medical Exit

A contestant may be forced to leave when the medical team determines that continuing would be unsafe. This category includes injuries, illness and other definitive medical decisions.

Elimination Challenge

Some challenges directly eliminate the contestant who finishes last or fails to complete the objective. The exit therefore depends on the challenge result rather than a vote.

Voluntary Withdrawal

A contestant may voluntarily leave the show for personal, psychological, family-related or physical reasons. This category is separate from a medically imposed withdrawal.

Ambassadors

At the merge, representatives of the former tribes may be required to designate a contestant for elimination. If they cannot agree, some seasons use a random draw or another procedure.

Orienteering

Orienteering is a final-stage search challenge. Contestants must locate a landmark and then find a dagger. Depending on the season’s format, the last one or two contestants who fail to find a dagger are eliminated.

Pole Challenge

Contestants must remain balanced for as long as possible on platforms that become progressively narrower. The winner chooses the person who will join them before the final jury.

Loss at the Final Jury

The finalists present their journeys to a jury made up of former contestants eliminated during the second part of the game, after the merge. The jury votes to select the winner; the other finalists are classified in this category.

Winner / Co-winner

The contestant receiving the most jury votes is considered the winner. Some editions produced co-winners; all are treated as winners in the dataset.

6. Conditional Elimination Probability by Phase

For each phase, the calculation includes only contestants still in the game at the beginning of that phase. A contestant eliminated within the first five exits is therefore not included in the denominator for the following phase.

* Raw data: proportions directly observed among contestants still present at the start of the phase. Adjusted data: estimated probabilities after simultaneously controlling for gender, age, physical profile and season.

Chart Observation

At the start of the game, the adjusted elimination probability is slightly higher for women than for men, especially during the first five eliminations. This pattern then weakens and reverses in the second half of the game, when men show the higher adjusted elimination probability.

Possible Explanation

This shift may be related to the gradual move from a collective logic to a more individual one. Early on, tribes may seek to preserve contestants perceived as the most useful in team challenges, which may disadvantage some women viewed as less physical. After the merge, competitors may increasingly target athletic or strategic threats, which are more often male in this sample. Alliances and personal affinities may also matter, but they are not directly measured here.

Chart Observation

Across the first two phases, contestants aged 18–25 and those aged 42 and over have the highest adjusted elimination probabilities. Between eliminations 11 and 15, the probability rises to roughly 54–60% for all three groups under 42, while falling to 27.5% for contestants aged 42 and over. In the final phase, the two age extremes reach elimination probabilities of approximately 85–86%.

Possible Explanation

Early on, contestants aged 42 and over may be more exposed if their tribe perceives them as less effective in certain challenges or more vulnerable to fatigue. Among 18–25-year-olds, vulnerability may be related to more limited social or strategic experience. The decline for contestants aged 42 and over in the third phase may reflect survivor selection: the older contestants still present are likely among the most resilient or best integrated. In the final phase, exits depend on orienteering, the pole challenge, the choice of co-finalist and the jury; the small number of contestants makes these estimates especially sensitive to a few individual journeys.

Chart Observation

In orienteering, adjusted elimination probabilities are similar for men and women. At the final jury, men show a slightly higher probability of losing. The largest difference appears in the pole challenge, where men are eliminated more often than women.

Possible Explanation

The pole challenge relies primarily on balance, static endurance, concentration and body-weight management rather than brute strength. This could favor certain lighter or more stable body types. There is also a selection effect: the women who reach this stage form a particularly resilient group. Finally, elimination also depends on the pole winner’s choice of co-finalist, which may reflect strategic and relational considerations.

No major difference is observed between physical and non-physical profiles in the pole challenge or at the final jury. The main gap appears in orienteering, where physical profiles have a substantially lower adjusted elimination probability.

Possible Explanation

Orienteering requires contestants to cover a large area, remain clear-headed and locate landmarks quickly. Better physical conditioning may help contestants cover more ground and resist fatigue, although the challenge also depends on navigation, method and composure. In the pole challenge, balance and concentration may matter more than power; at the final jury, social relationships and the overall assessment of a contestant’s journey become central.

Chart Observation

In orienteering, contestants aged 42 and over have the highest adjusted elimination probability. In the pole challenge, those aged 34–41 are the most exposed. At the final jury, the 18–25 and 42+ groups have the highest probabilities of defeat, while the 34–41 group has the lowest.

Possible Explanation

In orienteering, accumulated fatigue may affect some contestants aged 42 and over more strongly, although search method, navigation and composure remain essential. This interpretation should remain cautious because the sample is small and the dataset does not directly measure physiological fatigue.

The high elimination probability for contestants aged 34–41 in the pole challenge could also be explained by the winner’s strategic choice. In the sample studied, contestants in this age group who reach the final jury have only about a 13% adjusted probability of defeat, far below the other groups. They may therefore be perceived as particularly dangerous jury opponents, encouraging the pole winner not to choose them as co-finalists.

This theory remains exploratory. The number of finalists is very small, and the dataset does not contain the winner’s exact motivations when choosing whom to take to the final jury.

The high probabilities of defeat for the 18–25 and 42+ groups at the jury may also be related to their minority status. These groups are already less numerous at the start of the show and may be even more underrepresented by the final stage. A jury made up mainly of contestants from the middle age groups might, through affinity or generational identification, be more inclined to vote for someone closer to their own age.

Again, this is only a plausible hypothesis. The small number of juries and finalists does not allow a genuine age-affinity effect to be established. Votes may depend on many other factors, including personal relationships, strategy, perceived merit, betrayals or the quality of the final speech.

Chart Observation

Physical profiles have the highest adjusted probability of victory, ahead of non-physical profiles. The middle age groups, especially contestants aged 26–33, perform better than the 18–25 and 42+ groups. Women also have a higher adjusted probability of victory than men.

Possible Explanation

A physical profile may provide protection during the early phases and help in certain individual or final challenges. The middle age groups may benefit from a balance of physical ability, experience and social integration. Women’s higher observed probability may be related to being perceived as less threatening after the merge, their performance in the pole challenge or how their journey is evaluated by the jury. These mechanisms remain hypotheses: the differences do not demonstrate causality, and some are not statistically established.

9. Conclusion

This study shows that age, gender and physical profile are associated with contestants’ journeys in Koh-Lanta, but their effects vary across phases of the game.

Physical profile shows the most consistent pattern: physical contestants are generally less exposed to early elimination and have a higher adjusted probability of victory. Age also appears to matter, with the middle age groups generally performing better than the 18–25 and 42+ groups. The effect of gender is more variable, with differences changing by stage, especially during the pole challenge and the final phase.

These results should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously. The study covers only 17 seasons, several differences are not statistically significant, and the final stages involve few contestants. The conclusions should therefore be read as exploratory trends rather than general rules or demonstrated causal relationships.
